summary: Summarization hides details of individual prefixes in large networks. This document specifies a way to announce that a particular prefix covered by a summary is unreachable, enabling fast convergence by steering traffic away.

eli5.summary: If one house on a street is cut off, the street sign still says the street exists. This lets the network announce a specific house is unreachable.

questions: what is an unreachable prefix announcement
how does upa work in is-is
how does upa work in ospf
subtitle: A way for routers to announce that one prefix inside a summary route has become unreachable.

tldr.problem: Summarization hides individual prefixes, so routers outside an area or domain never learn that one prefix covered by a summary has become unreachable.
tldr.mechanism: An ABR or ASBR advertises the prefix with a metric that excludes it from route calculation and sets a new U-flag (and optionally an UP-flag for planned events) in IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
tldr.outcome: Receiving routers can react quickly, for example by triggering BGP PIC Edge. UPA is an optional, event-driven signal and is disabled by default.

today: RFC 9929 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2026. It is not obsoleted or updated by any later RFC. It relies on RFC 9792 for the OSPF prefix flag encoding.

sections.title: Why Summaries Need an Unreachable Signal
sections.content:
Link-state IGPs such as IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 spread routing information inside one Autonomous System. Every router in an area builds a Link State Database (LSDB) from what the routers advertise.

To scale, networks are split into levels or areas and domains, and summarization combines several contiguous networks into one larger summary route. The cost is that the state of individual prefixes is suppressed. That state is useful for triggering fast-convergence mechanisms outside the IGP, such as BGP Prefix-Independent Convergence (PIC).

The same problem appears in maintenance. A node is drained before it is taken down, by using the OVERLOAD bit in IS-IS, the H-bit in OSPFv2 or the R-bit in OSPFv3. When an Area Border Router (ABR) or Autonomous System Boundary Router (ASBR) summarizes those prefixes, nodes outside the area or domain do not learn that they became unreachable.

Normally an IGP just withdraws an advertisement to show a prefix is gone. That cannot work when the prefix was never advertised separately because the summary covered it. The Unreachable Prefix Announcement (UPA) fills that gap, and the document says it does so in a backward-compatible manner.
sections.eli5: When many houses share one street name, nobody hears if a single house loses its road. UPA is a way to shout about just that house.

sections.title: When a UPA Is Generated
sections.content:
An ABR or ASBR MAY generate a UPA for a prefix covered by a summary it originates in two cases. One is that a previously reachable prefix becomes unreachable. The other is planned maintenance: the originating node signals overload (IS-IS), the H-bit (OSPFv2) or the R-bit (OSPFv3), or the metric to the prefix crosses a configured threshold.

Generation and propagation are optional, SHOULD be controlled by a configuration knob and SHOULD be disabled by default. Implementations MAY limit UPAs to specific prefixes, such as host prefixes or SRv6 locators.

A UPA is an event-driven signal of a destination going from reachable to unreachable, not a persistent state. The ABR or ASBR MUST withdraw it when the reason ceases. Even if the reason persists, it SHOULD be withdrawn after some time, long enough for network-wide flooding and action, since stale UPAs would stay in every router's LSDB. A configurable lifetime and a configurable limit on how many UPAs are originated at once are both called for.

In IS-IS the unit of flooding is the LSP, so UPAs are RECOMMENDED to go in dedicated LSPs. OSPF advertises each inter-area and external prefix in its own LSA, so that concern does not apply.
sections.eli5: The notice should only go up when something just broke or is about to be fixed, and it should come down again after a while so old news does not pile up.

sections.title: UPA in IS-IS
sections.content:
IS-IS already lets a prefix be advertised with a metric larger than 0xFE000000, which keeps it out of normal SPF computation (RFC 5305 for IPv4, RFC 5308 for IPv6). A UPA in IS-IS MUST use such a metric. Nodes that do not support UPA ignore it in route calculation but still flood it, so not every node needs an upgrade.

Because high metrics may be used for other reasons, two new bits in the prefix attribute flags of RFC 7794 make the meaning explicit:

  • U-Flag (bit 5): the prefix is unreachable.
  • UP-Flag (bit 6): the prefix is unreachable due to a planned event. The originator MUST NOT set it without the U-Flag, and receivers MUST ignore it if the U-Flag is not set.

If the metric is less than or equal to 0xFE000000, both flags MUST be ignored. UPA is supported in all the prefix reachability TLVs in the IS-IS registry, for example SRv6 Locator, Extended IP reachability, MT IP Reach, IPv6 IP Reach, MT IPv6 IP Reach and the IPv4 and IPv6 Algorithm Prefix Reachability TLVs.

For propagation, L1/L2 routers must recognize UPAs. Normally a prefix is only propagated from a level where it is reachable, but that requirement MUST NOT apply to UPAs. The original metric MUST be preserved and the cost to reach the originator MUST NOT be considered.
sections.eli5: IS-IS already has a way to write an address in a book with a cost so high that nobody uses it. UPA adds a sticker that says this is on purpose because the place cannot be reached.

sections.title: UPA in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
sections.content:
OSPF already has LSInfinity, the all-ones 24-bit metric 0xffffff that marks a destination as unreachable in summary-LSAs and AS-external-LSAs. OSPFv3 also has the NU-bit in PrefixOptions, which keeps a prefix out of the routing calculation.

An ABR or ASBR advertising a UPA MUST set the LSA age to a value lower than MaxAge and the metric to LSInfinity. Flooding inside the area follows the existing procedures.

To tell UPA from other uses of those values, two new bits are defined in the Prefix Attribute Flags Sub-TLV from RFC 9792: U-Flag (bit 0) and UP-Flag (bit 1), with the same rule that UP requires U.

  • OSPFv2: the metric MUST be LSInfinity or both flags are ignored. For default algorithm 0, the unreachable prefix must be advertised in the base LSA, such as a Summary-LSA, AS-external-LSA or NSSA AS-external LSA.
  • OSPFv3: the metric must be LSInfinity in the parent TLV (or in the IP Algorithm Prefix Reachability sub-TLV for flexible algorithm prefixes), and the NU-bit MUST be set in the parent TLV PrefixOptions. Otherwise both flags are ignored.

OSPFv3 prefixes in the non-extended LSAs are signaled using the corresponding extended LSAs, which needs the sparse mode of RFC 8362.

ABRs and ASBRs MAY pass UPAs between areas or domains, keeping the original LSInfinity metric, with no requirement that the prefix be reachable in the source area and no use of the cost to the originator.
sections.eli5: OSPF already has a way to say a place is infinitely far away. UPA adds a sticker saying why, and rules so that only real notices are believed.

sections.title: Processing a UPA
sections.content:
Handling received UPAs is optional and SHOULD be controlled by configuration at the receiver. The receiver decides what to use the UPA for and which applications to notify. How it is used is outside the scope of the document. One example given is triggering BGP PIC Edge.

Applications cannot infer from the absence of a UPA that reachability has returned. They must use their own mechanisms to verify the remote endpoint.
sections.eli5: Hearing the notice is up to each listener. If the notice disappears, that does not mean the house is reachable again, so listeners must check on their own.

sections.title: Area and Domain Partition
sections.content:
UPA is not meant to solve a partition of an area or domain. When one partitions while several ABRs or ASBRs advertise the same summary, each can reach only part of the summarized range, so traffic may be dropped or delivered depending on which one it enters through.

UPA does not make this worse. Each ABR or ASBR generates UPAs for the destinations it lost locally. Outside nodes may then choose another egress node. If that node is outside the partitioned area, traffic is restored. If it is inside and covered by the summary, traffic entering through an ABR or ASBR that cannot reach it is still dropped, as it would be without UPA.
sections.eli5: If a street is split in two, the notice does not fix the break. It only helps cars choose another route when another route exists.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
An attacker could inject a false but apparently valid UPA. The document says this risk is no greater than that of injecting any other false advertisement. Existing security extensions reduce it: RFC 5304, RFC 5310 and RFC 7794 for IS-IS; RFC 2328, RFC 7474 and RFC 7684 for OSPFv2; RFC 5340, RFC 4552 and RFC 8362 for OSPFv3.

IANA adds bit 5 (U-Flag) and bit 6 (UP-Flag) to the IS-IS prefix attribute flags registry, and bit 0 (U-Flag) and bit 1 (UP-Flag) to the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 Prefix Extended Flags registries.
sections.eli5: Someone could post a fake notice, but they could already post other fake notices, and the usual locks on the network help here too.
